clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic FA2H variants, also termed fatty acid hydroxylase-associated neurodegeneration (FAHN)
Usually presents in childhood with spastic gait that progresses to include dystonia, ataxia and cognitive decline
It falls within the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum, with pallidal iron deposition on susceptibility imaging
MRI characteristically shows a leukodystrophy-like white-matter change together with cerebellar and pontine atrophy
FA2H encodes fatty acid 2-hydroxylase, essential for producing hydroxylated galactolipids of myelin
Optic atrophy and seizures may develop as the disorder advances
Management is symptomatic, addressing spasticity, dystonia, mobility, seizures and nutrition
reference.pathophysiology: SPG35 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in FA2H, which encodes fatty acid 2-hydroxylase, an enzyme that generates 2-hydroxylated fatty acids incorporated into the galactosylceramide and sulfatide lipids of myelin. Deficient hydroxylation destabilises myelin lipid composition and disturbs oligodendrocyte and neuronal membrane homeostasis, producing a hypomyelinating and demyelinating leukodystrophy-like process with secondary iron accumulation in the globus pallidus. This widespread disturbance affects corticospinal tracts, cerebellum, basal ganglia and optic pathways, generating the complicated phenotype of spasticity with dystonia, ataxia, cognitive decline and visual failure.
additionalDifferentials: Other neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation disorders (PKAN, PLAN)
Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other inherited leukodystrophies
SPG11 and SPG15 complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia
Wilson disease and other treatable dystonia-parkinsonism mimics
additionalInvestigations: FA2H sequencing within a complicated-HSP or leukodystrophy panel
MRI of brain including iron-sensitive (susceptibility-weighted) sequences
Metabolic and copper studies to exclude treatable mimics
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dystonia or bulbar involvement affecting swallowing and speech
New or worsening seizures requiring urgent management
Visual deterioration indicating optic pathway involvement
Loss of independent mobility signalling disease progression
reference.prognosis: SPG35 is a progressive childhood-onset neurodegenerative disorder, and most affected children develop increasing spasticity, dystonia and cognitive impairment with loss of independent walking over time.
pitfalls: Not requesting iron-sensitive MRI sequences and missing the brain iron accumulation clue
Misclassifying the disorder as a pure hereditary spastic paraplegia early in its course
Overlooking treatable mimics such as Wilson disease before confirming the genetic cause
Underestimating the multidisciplinary needs of an evolving leukodystrophy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, with intrathecal baclofen for severe tone
Manage dystonia with anticholinergic agents, botulinum toxin injection or deep-brain-stimulation assessment in refractory cases
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses, seating and rehabilitation for the combined spastic, dystonic and ataxic gait disorder
Antiseizure medication for seizures, with neuropsychological support and carer education for progressive cognitive decline
Ophthalmology and low-vision support for optic atrophy
Nutritional and swallow assessment as bulbar function declines, with enteral feeding support if required
Genetic counselling with cascade FA2H testing for autosomal recessive inheritance
